Marfanoid Habitus: Marfan or Homocystinuria?

A tall, thin child with a clot or learning problems, especially with fair skin, needs a homocysteine level before Marfan is called

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

A Marfanoid child: look for what Marfan does not do.

  • Intellectual disability, a thrombotic stroke or clot, fair skin and hair, lens dislocated down: homocystinuria. Plasma homocysteine and methionine are both high.
  • Normal intellect, lens up and out, aortic root dilation: Marfan syndrome. Echocardiographic surveillance and a beta-blocker or angiotensin receptor blocker.
  • Stretchy skin, easy bruising and lax joints with normal proportions: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, not a Marfanoid disorder.

Treat homocystinuria with pyridoxine (B6) first (about half respond), plus folate and vitamin B12 (cobalamin); nonresponders need methionine restriction and betaine. Never nitrous oxide.

Diagnosis
Marfanoid child: which one?
FeatureMarfan syndromeHomocystinuria
InheritanceAutosomal dominant; fibrillin-1 gene (FBN1)Autosomal recessive (cystathionine beta-synthase)
LensUp and outDown
IntellectNormalOften impaired
VesselsAortic root dilation, dissectionClots: stroke, DVT (deep vein thrombosis), PE (pulmonary embolism)
Skin, hair, jointsUsual coloring; joints often laxFair, fine hair; joints often stiff, not lax
Decoys Ehlers-Danlos – lax joints, hyperextensible skin, fragile tissue; vascular EDS (Ehlers-Danlos syndrome) ruptures arteries rather than clotting them; no Marfanoid build or learning problems · Phenylketonuria – fair skin and intellectual disability, with a musty odor and eczema; no Marfanoid build or clots
Management and treatment
By situation Homocystinuria – pyridoxine trial; folate and B12; methionine restriction and betaine if B6 fails · Surgery – avoid nitrous oxide: it inhibits methionine synthase, raises homocysteine and invites thrombosis · Marfan – echocardiographic surveillance of the aortic root; beta-blocker or angiotensin receptor blocker
Practice
  1. 5-year-old girl with sudden weakness of the right arm and leg developmental delay; fair skin long, thin limbs; low upper-to-lower segment ratio Joint hyperlaxity T 37.0 °C · MRI: left middle cerebral artery infarct → Homocystinuria → a Marfanoid child with a stroke, developmental delay and fair skin has homocystinuria; joint laxity fits Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos and is atypical for homocystinuria (joints usually stiff), but neither explains the stroke, delay or fair skin; check plasma homocysteine and methionine
  2. 18-year-old man, 195 cm tall, with pectus excavatum both lenses subluxed upward normal intellect; no clots ever Arm span exceeds height; father also very tall BP 124/70 mm Hg · echocardiogram: aortic root 4.8 cm → Marfan syndrome → tall with pectus, upward lens subluxation, normal intellect and a dilated aortic root is Marfan syndrome (autosomal dominant, FBN1): echocardiographic surveillance and a beta-blocker or angiotensin receptor blocker
  3. 12-year-old girl with recurrent shoulder and knee dislocations since age 8 velvety, hyperextensible skin bruises easily; wide, thin scars Normal height and proportions; normal school performance T 36.9 °C · lenses in place → Ehlers-Danlos syndrome → joint laxity with stretchy, fragile skin and normal proportions and intellect is Ehlers-Danlos syndrome: genetic testing for the collagen defect
  4. 8-year-old boy was diagnosed with homocystinuria last week plasma homocysteine and methionine both high downward lens dislocation; tall, thin; learning support at school No clot so far T 37.0 °C · B12 and folate normal → Pyridoxine with assessment for B6 responsiveness → first try pyridoxine and test the response (about half respond), with folate and B12; nonresponders need methionine restriction and betaine
  5. 16-year-old boy, tall and thin with long fingers both lenses subluxed struggles in school; repeated a grade No family history of sudden death BP 118/72 mm Hg · slit lamp: direction unclear → Serum homocysteine level → a Marfanoid build with lens subluxation fits Marfan and homocystinuria; serum (plasma) homocysteine separates them, and it comes before echocardiography or FBN1 testing when learning problems or clots are present
  6. 10-year-old girl was diagnosed with homocystinuria at 4 on pyridoxine, folate and B12 scheduled for dental surgery under general anesthesia Parents ask what the anesthesiologist must avoid T 37.0 °C · homocysteine near target → Nitrous oxide anesthesia → nitrous oxide inhibits methionine synthase (a B12 enzyme), raises homocysteine and invites perioperative thrombosis; avoid it
Pairs with Water-Soluble Vitamin Deficiency: acquired high homocysteine (methylmalonic acid high in B12 deficiency, normal in folate). Inherited Tumor Syndromes: the Marfanoid habitus of MEN2B (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B).
Transferable rule

When a lookalike syndrome is on the table, list what the classic one cannot do; any such finding moves the answer.
